messages.content: I want mobile manipulators to reposition unseen furniture while maintaining contact. The key challenge is distinguishing object slip from localization drift when the visual view is intermittently occluded.

The goal combines contact-preserving furniture repositioning with a specific diagnostic distinction: the manipulator needs to tell whether apparent movement reflects object slip or drift in its localization estimate. It must do so despite intermittent visual occlusion. The stated targets are repositioning unseen furniture within 5 cm in 90% of trials, and identifying slip versus localization drift with 90% balanced accuracy without external tracking during execution.
What is the distinction between slip and localization drift here?

Conceptually, object slip concerns movement of the furniture relative to the contact being maintained. Localization drift concerns an error that develops in the manipulator’s estimate of location. Both could complicate interpretation of where the furniture is, but they are not the same event: one concerns the physical contact relationship, while the other concerns an estimate. The goal is to distinguish them, not merely detect that something appears to have changed.
Does slip necessarily mean contact has already been lost?

No. Movement relative to a contact can occur while contact remains. That matters here because maintaining contact is part of the repositioning goal; distinguishing slip from drift should not be understood as requiring the manipulator to let go of the furniture.
And the localization part refers to the manipulator’s estimate, rather than automatically to physical motion of the furniture?

Yes. If an estimate drifts, the estimated location changes or becomes inaccurate; that alone does not establish that the furniture slipped. Conversely, a real slip should not simply be attributed to an inaccurate estimate. The requested distinction is between those two explanations, without presuming that an apparent change proves either one.
How should I read “unseen furniture”? Does it mean the furniture cannot be viewed at any point during a trial?

The goal calls for repositioning unseen furniture, but it does not say the furniture must remain completely invisible throughout execution. It separately specifies intermittent visual occlusion, which describes interruptions to the visual view rather than a requirement of continuous invisibility. The statement does not further define what counts as unseen or specify a particular furniture category.
So intermittent occlusion is a condition the repositioning target has to withstand?

Exactly. The within-5-cm target applies to trials with intermittent visual occlusion. That condition should remain explicit: it would change the stated requirement to discuss the accuracy target only for trials with an uninterrupted view. The goal does not specify when the occlusions occur or how long they last.
Can you unpack “within 5 cm in 90% of trials” without assuming a particular test setup?

It is a trial-level repositioning target: in at least 90% of trials, the repositioning outcome should be within 5 cm of the intended outcome. The statement does not define the number of trials, a distance-measurement convention, or an additional orientation tolerance. Those details should not be silently supplied when restating the target.
Does that mean every individual repositioning has to be within 5 cm?

No. The requirement sets a 90% success rate across trials, not a guarantee for every trial. The 5 cm value is the tolerance used to judge whether a trial meets the repositioning target; the 90% value describes how often that must happen.
The other 90% is a different kind of measurement, right?

Right. The second target is 90% balanced accuracy for identifying slip versus localization drift. It measures the distinction between those conditions, whereas the first 90% concerns how often repositioning finishes within 5 cm. Meeting one figure does not, by itself, establish the other.
Why specify balanced accuracy instead of just accuracy?

For a two-class distinction, balanced accuracy is the average of the rate of correctly identifying slip and the rate of correctly identifying localization drift. Unlike ordinary overall accuracy, it does not let a more frequent class dominate the score merely because it appears more often. The goal specifies 90% for that balanced measure; it does not provide the separate rates for the two conditions.
Would 90% balanced accuracy require exactly 90% correct identification for each condition?

Not necessarily. As a purely arithmetic illustration, rates of 95% for one condition and 85% for the other average to 90%. Those numbers are not results or proposed targets for either condition here; they only show why a balanced-accuracy value does not determine both component rates.
What does the restriction on external tracking cover?

The identification target is to distinguish slip from localization drift without external tracking during execution. In other words, the stated diagnostic capability cannot depend on an external tracker while the repositioning is being carried out. The goal does not name the inputs the manipulator would use instead, nor does it specify an evaluation procedure.
Is intermittent visual occlusion the same restriction as having no external tracking?

No. Intermittent visual occlusion concerns interruptions to the visual view during the furniture task. The external-tracking restriction concerns how slip and localization drift are identified during execution. Both conditions belong in the description, but one should not be substituted for the other.
Could I state the aim as merely detecting an error while moving furniture?

That would be too broad. The aim is to distinguish object slip specifically from localization drift while maintaining contact during furniture repositioning. It also includes the two numerical targets: within 5 cm in 90% of trials on unseen furniture with intermittent visual occlusion, and 90% balanced accuracy for the slip-versus-drift identification without external tracking during execution.
Does the goal already select a way to make that distinction?

No method is specified. It states the capability, the operating conditions, and the performance targets, but not a sensor arrangement, diagnostic algorithm, contact strategy, or motion procedure. Describing any one of those as the chosen approach would go beyond the goal.

A possible approach is contact-constrained factor-graph fusion of wrist shear, odometry, and intermittent RGB-D to distinguish slip from drift during furniture repositioning. Can you unpack that proposal?

It proposes combining three sources of information rather than treating any one of them as decisive. Wrist shear provides information about forces at the manipulator’s contact, odometry provides an estimate of the robot’s motion, and intermittent RGB-D provides visual and depth information when a view is available. A factor graph is a way to represent how observations and estimated quantities relate. “Contact-constrained” means the contact relationship is part of that reasoning while the furniture is being repositioned. This is a proposed approach, not a demonstrated result.
Why might combining those sources help with slip versus localization drift?

The two explanations concern different things: slip involves the physical relationship at contact, while localization drift involves the estimated location. Looking at wrist shear, odometry, and available RGB-D together could provide more context for that distinction than interpreting an apparent position change alone. The proposal does not claim that any particular pattern across the three sources definitively identifies one explanation.
What role does the wrist shear information play?

It brings contact-related information into the proposed fusion. Because the manipulator is maintaining contact during repositioning, that information may be relevant when considering whether movement at the contact has occurred. Wrist shear is not, by itself, a stated slip label: the proposal is to interpret it alongside odometry and intermittent RGB-D.
And odometry is there to account for the manipulator’s own movement?

Yes. Odometry supplies an estimate of motion that can help interpret changes observed during repositioning. But an odometry-based estimate is still an estimate, so it cannot simply be treated as an unquestionable reference when the question includes localization drift. Its role in this proposal is as one input to fusion, not as a guaranteed ground truth.
What exactly does intermittent RGB-D contribute if the view can be occluded?

RGB-D refers to visual information with depth information. “Intermittent” acknowledges that such information is available only at some times, rather than assuming an uninterrupted visual stream. In the proposed fusion, available RGB-D can contribute information when there is a view, while the formulation must still make sense when the view is temporarily unavailable. The proposal does not specify an occlusion schedule or how particular images would be processed.
Does a factor graph mean the system makes a decision from each sensor independently and then votes?

Not necessarily. The proposal is for fusion in a factor-graph formulation: a shared representation of relationships among observations and estimates. That is different from saying that wrist shear, odometry, and RGB-D each make a separate final decision and that their decisions are counted as votes. The exact variables, relationships, and decision rule are not specified.
Could you explain “contact-constrained” without assuming a particular mathematical model?

At a conceptual level, it means that reasoning about motion should respect the fact that the manipulator is in contact with the furniture. The contact relationship provides relevant context for interpreting estimated motion and possible slip. The phrase does not specify a particular equation, a particular contact model, or how strongly a constraint would be applied.
Would a contact constraint amount to assuming slip cannot happen?

No. That would undermine the purpose of distinguishing slip from localization drift. Maintaining contact does not mean that nothing can move relative to that contact. The proposal calls for contact-constrained reasoning about the distinction, not for ruling out slip in advance.
So the graph is not just a way to smooth the odometry?

Correct. Odometry is one of the named inputs, but the proposal is to fuse it with wrist shear and intermittent RGB-D under contact constraints. Its stated purpose is to distinguish slip from drift during furniture repositioning. It does not say the entire method reduces to adjusting an odometry estimate.
If RGB-D becomes unavailable during an occlusion, does the proposal say to stop repositioning?

It does not say that. Intermittent RGB-D is explicitly part of the proposal, so continuous visual availability should not be assumed. At the same time, the statement does not prescribe what the manipulator does during any particular occlusion or guarantee that the remaining information always resolves the distinction.
Would an RGB-D reading on its own establish that the furniture slipped?

No. The point of the proposal is to interpret intermittent RGB-D together with wrist shear, odometry, and the contact relationship. A change in visual or depth information alone would not automatically separate physical slip from an error in an estimated location. The proposal does not give a standalone visual test for slip.
How does this relate to keeping contact while repositioning, rather than diagnosing movement afterward?

The proposed distinction is made in the context of furniture repositioning while contact is maintained. It is not presented merely as an after-the-fact interpretation of a completed move. The proposal does not, however, spell out the timing of estimates or any specific action taken in response to them.
Does mentioning RGB-D mean the approach relies on external tracking during execution?

Not on the information given. The proposal names intermittent RGB-D as an input; it does not identify an external tracking system or specify where the RGB-D observations come from. The stated identification target remains distinguishing slip from localization drift without external tracking during execution. The proposal alone should not be taken as proof that a particular implementation meets that restriction.
Could I say this method achieves the within-5-cm repositioning target?

Not yet. This is a proposed way to distinguish slip from drift during repositioning, not a report of performance. The goal includes repositioning unseen furniture within 5 cm in 90% of trials with intermittent visual occlusion, but no result for the proposed fusion is stated.
What about the 90% balanced-accuracy target for identifying slip versus drift?

That remains a target, not an established performance figure for this proposal. Balanced accuracy concerns the two identification conditions rather than repositioning distance. Nothing here supplies measured rates, so the proposal cannot be described as having attained 90% balanced accuracy.
What is the most careful one-sentence description of the idea?

Use contact-constrained factor-graph fusion of wrist shear, odometry, and intermittent RGB-D as a proposed way to distinguish object slip from localization drift while a mobile manipulator maintains contact during furniture repositioning.
Is there anything in that sentence that specifies the graph’s variables or how slip is classified?

No. It identifies the formulation, the three information sources, the contact context, and the intended distinction. It leaves the graph’s detailed representation and the classification procedure open rather than claiming that either has already been defined.
During three-second visual occlusions, which wrist-shear and contact-kinematic cues could distinguish gripper slip from base-pose drift?

The distinction to look for is between a change at the gripper–furniture contact and a change in the estimated base pose. A potentially informative wrist-shear cue would be a change associated with apparent relative motion at the contact. A potentially informative contact-kinematic cue would be a mismatch between the motion expected if that contact remains fixed and the motion inferred while repositioning. Base-pose drift, by contrast, can change the estimated world-frame positions without requiring physical motion at the gripper contact. These are candidate cues, not a specified or validated rule for diagnosing either condition during a three-second occlusion.
Does a change in wrist shear by itself identify gripper slip?

No. Wrist shear is contact-related information, but a change in it alone does not establish that the gripper moved relative to the furniture. The question is whether that information, considered with the contact kinematics, is more consistent with relative movement at the contact or with a changed pose estimate. The question supplies no shear threshold or distinctive signal pattern that would make a single reading decisive.
What do you mean by contact kinematics here?

Here it means the motion relationship implied by the gripper remaining in contact with the furniture. If the assumed contact relationship and the estimated motions no longer fit together, that inconsistency is relevant. The inconsistency does not automatically say which estimate is wrong or prove that slip occurred; it is something to interpret alongside wrist shear and the possibility of base-pose drift.
Could an apparent movement of the contact point just be caused by a drifting base pose?

Yes, if the apparent movement is expressed using an inaccurate base-pose estimate. A change in an estimated world-frame contact location need not mean the gripper physically slipped. The important distinction is between apparent motion arising from the reference estimate and physical relative motion at the gripper–furniture contact.
So should I treat relative motion at the gripper as the deciding cue?

Physical relative motion there is central to what gripper slip means. The difficulty during visual occlusion is establishing that such motion actually occurred, rather than merely inferring it from an estimate that may have drifted. A contact-kinematic inconsistency can raise the question, but without a specified way to resolve the competing explanations, it should not be called a deciding cue.
How would wrist shear help interpret that inconsistency?

It offers contact-related evidence that can be considered alongside the kinematic relationship. If both indicate a change associated with the contact, that may make a slip interpretation more plausible than it would be from an apparent world-frame position change alone. But the question does not establish a one-to-one correspondence between a shear change and slip, or say how much agreement is enough to make a classification.
What if the estimated base position changes, but the contact-related cues don't indicate a change?

That contrast could be more consistent with base-pose drift than with gripper slip: the estimated reference has changed without corresponding evidence of changed contact. It would still be a cautious interpretation, not proof. A lack of an obvious wrist-shear or contact-kinematic cue does not, by itself, rule out slip.
And if the contact-kinematic relationship seems to change at the same time as the wrist shear?

That combination would make gripper slip worth considering because both observations concern the contact rather than only the base's estimated pose. It still leaves open whether the observations can be interpreted unambiguously. No specific temporal pattern, magnitude, or classification criterion is given for a three-second occlusion.
Does the three-second duration tell us which cue is most reliable?

No. It defines the visual-occlusion interval in the question. It does not provide measurements, error characteristics, or a comparison showing that wrist shear or contact kinematics is more reliable over that interval. Any claim that one cue reliably wins after three seconds would add information that has not been supplied.
Can RGB-D settle the issue within those three seconds?

The interval is described as a visual occlusion, so visual information should not be assumed available to settle the distinction during it. Intermittent RGB-D is part of the proposed fusion context, but this question focuses on what wrist shear and contact kinematics can indicate while the view is occluded. It does not say what visual information is available immediately before or after a particular interval.
Is base-pose drift the same thing as the furniture moving?

No. Base-pose drift is an error in the estimated pose of the mobile base. Furniture movement is physical movement of the object. An inaccurate base-pose estimate can make positions expressed relative to that estimate appear inconsistent without establishing that the furniture moved relative to the gripper.
Could both gripper slip and base-pose drift occur during an occlusion?

Conceptually, yes; they are different phenomena, so one does not logically exclude the other. The question asks which cues distinguish them, but it does not state whether simultaneous occurrences are considered or how such a case would be labeled. It would be unsafe to assume the two explanations are always mutually exclusive in the physical situation.
Does maintaining contact rule out gripper slip in this question?

No. Maintaining contact does not require the contact location to remain unchanged relative to the furniture. The distinction remains meaningful precisely because relative movement can be considered without assuming that contact has been lost.
Can you put the useful contrast in a compact form?

A change that appears only in the base-referenced pose estimate points toward possible base-pose drift; contact-kinematic evidence of relative movement at the gripper, especially when considered with wrist-shear changes, points toward possible gripper slip. Neither pattern is stated to be conclusive. During the three-second visual occlusions, the open question is which of those cues actually separates the two explanations.

Here is a hypothesis for the three-second visual occlusions: contact residuals accompanied by wrist-shear spikes indicate gripper slip, whereas contact residuals without those spikes indicate base-pose drift, at ≥90% balanced accuracy.

That is a specific, testable hypothesis about the two cues. In both cases, a contact residual is present; the proposed discriminator is whether it is accompanied by a wrist-shear spike. The hypothesis predicts gripper slip for residuals with spikes and base-pose drift for residuals without spikes during three-second visual occlusions, with at least 90% balanced accuracy. It is a predicted level of performance, not an observed result.
Why does the hypothesis require a contact residual in both cases?

Because it addresses how to interpret a contact-related inconsistency, rather than claiming that a shear spike alone diagnoses slip. The residual is the common condition; the presence or absence of a shear spike supplies the proposed distinction. Nothing in the hypothesis says how to classify an interval with no contact residual.
What does “contact residual” mean without specifying a particular equation?

Conceptually, it is a mismatch between what the contact relationship would imply and what the estimated motion or observations indicate. Here it serves as the contact-kinematic cue. The hypothesis does not define its calculation, units, or the magnitude needed for it to count as present.
Does “with shear spikes” mean the residual itself spikes?

No. The hypothesis names two distinct things: contact residuals and spikes in wrist shear. It proposes interpreting a contact residual differently depending on whether a wrist-shear spike accompanies it. It does not specify the size or shape of either signal.
If there is a residual and a shear spike, can I state that slip has been established?

Not as an established fact. The hypothesis says that combination indicates gripper slip; whether it does so reliably has not been shown here. “Predicted to indicate slip” preserves the hypothesis’s meaning without presenting its proposed classification as a confirmed diagnosis.
What if there is a contact residual but no spike?

Under the hypothesis, that pattern indicates base-pose drift. Again, it is a proposed interpretation, not proof that drift occurred or proof that gripper slip did not occur. The ≥90% balanced-accuracy claim itself allows for classification errors.
Is “no spike” the same as “no wrist shear”?

No. The hypothesis contrasts a spike with its absence; it does not require wrist shear to be zero when no spike is detected. Nor does it define what would qualify as a spike, so the distinction should not be turned into an unstated numerical shear threshold.
Does the hypothesis say that every shear spike signals slip?
No. Its slip pattern is a contact residual accompanied by a shear spike. It does not make a claim about spikes when there is no contact residual, or about every possible wrist-shear fluctuation.
Do the residual and spike have to occur at precisely the same instant?

The hypothesis says the residuals are “with” shear spikes during three-second occlusions, but it does not define a timing window or require exact simultaneity. Adding a precise synchronization rule would be an additional specification, not something already contained in the hypothesis.
Why keep the three-second condition explicit?

It limits the prediction to three-second visual occlusions. The hypothesis does not establish the same distinction, or the same balanced accuracy, for shorter or longer occlusions or for uninterrupted visual observation. The duration and the visual-occlusion condition are part of what is being asserted.
Is ≥90% balanced accuracy an accuracy figure for repositioning furniture?

No. Here it is the hypothesized performance for distinguishing gripper slip from base-pose drift using those cue patterns during three-second occlusions. It is separate from the goal of repositioning unseen furniture within 5 cm in 90% of trials with intermittent visual occlusion. This hypothesis does not claim a measured repositioning outcome.
Could the predicted balanced accuracy reach 90% while one of the two conditions is identified less accurately than 90%?

Yes. Balanced accuracy averages the correct-identification rates for slip and drift. A value of at least 90% does not, by itself, assert that each rate individually reaches 90%. The hypothesis supplies no separate rate for either condition.
Does this tell us that residuals without spikes are always drift?

No. It proposes that they indicate drift with an overall balanced-accuracy target of at least 90% for the distinction. “Always” would assert a certainty that the hypothesis neither states nor supports.
How does this sharpen the question about wrist-shear and contact-kinematic cues?

It offers a particular answer to examine: first consider contact residuals, then use the presence or absence of accompanying wrist-shear spikes to distinguish gripper slip from base-pose drift during three-second visual occlusions. That is more specific than asking generally which cues matter, but it remains a hypothesis rather than a validated decision rule.
Does it prescribe how the factor graph combines the cues?

No. The broader proposal involves contact-constrained fusion, but this hypothesis states a predicted relationship between contact residuals, wrist-shear spikes, and the two interpretations. It does not give graph variables, factor definitions, a spike detector, or a classification algorithm.
Can the hypothesis be repeated in one sentence without sounding like a result?

The hypothesis is that, during three-second visual occlusions, contact residuals accompanied by wrist-shear spikes indicate gripper slip, while contact residuals without such spikes indicate base-pose drift, yielding ≥90% balanced accuracy for that distinction.
I’d like to record FurnitureContact-1 with induced grip slip and odometry drift during three-second visual occlusions, then fit shear-conditioned residuals and evaluate balanced accuracy.

That is a plan for examining whether contact-related inconsistencies, interpreted in light of wrist shear, can distinguish grip slip from odometry drift. FurnitureContact-1 is the recording named in the plan; the two induced conditions are grip slip and odometry drift during three-second visual occlusions. The subsequent work is to fit shear-conditioned residuals and evaluate balanced accuracy. None of those steps is reported as completed.
What does recording both induced conditions contribute to the question?

It gives the planned evaluation both kinds of event the distinction is meant to address. Grip slip concerns a change at the gripper’s contact with the furniture; odometry drift concerns an error in the motion estimate. Considering both during the stated occlusions makes it possible to ask whether the residuals, when interpreted with shear, distinguish those explanations. The plan does not yet say how well they do.
Does induced odometry drift mean physically moving the robot base?

Not necessarily. Odometry drift concerns the estimated motion, whereas physical movement of the base is a different thing. The plan says to induce odometry drift but does not specify how that induction is carried out, so it should not be rewritten as a particular physical movement or a particular way of altering measurements.
And does induced grip slip mean the manipulator lets go?

No such loss of contact is specified. Grip slip refers to relative movement at the grip; it need not mean the gripper has released the furniture altogether. The plan names induced grip slip without specifying its magnitude or a procedure for producing it.
Is FurnitureContact-1 an existing result?

The statement is a plan to record FurnitureContact-1. It does not report an existing completed recording, its contents, its size, or any result obtained from it. Treating the name as a completed dataset would go beyond what the plan states.
Why specify three-second occlusions rather than just saying visual occlusions?

The three-second duration is an explicit condition of the planned recording. It keeps the question focused on the interval in which the visual view is unavailable for that length of time. The plan does not say that findings from those intervals would automatically apply to other occlusion durations.
Does the plan say whether the occlusions happen at the start or end of a repositioning movement?

No. It specifies three-second visual occlusions during the recording, but not their placement within a repositioning movement or the timing of an induced condition within an occlusion. Those details should remain unspecified rather than being inferred.
Can you explain “shear-conditioned residuals” in ordinary language?

A residual is an inconsistency between a relationship being considered and the motion or observations used to assess it. “Shear-conditioned” means the planned fitting takes wrist-shear information into account when interpreting those residuals. The phrase does not supply a formula, a fitted model, or a numerical shear cutoff.
So is the plan to use shear spikes as an already fixed classification rule?

The plan says to fit shear-conditioned residuals and evaluate balanced accuracy. It does not specify a fixed spike detector, a threshold, or a final classification rule. Shear is part of the proposed interpretation of residuals, but the details of the fit are not stated.
What is being fitted: wrist shear itself or the relationship between shear and residuals?

The wording points to fitting residuals conditioned on shear: the residuals are considered in relation to wrist-shear information. It does not identify the mathematical form of that relationship or say that wrist shear alone is the quantity being fitted. The safe description is simply “fit shear-conditioned residuals.”
Does a contact residual necessarily mean grip slip in the planned recording?

No. The distinction being evaluated is grip slip versus odometry drift, so a residual cannot be assumed to prove slip on its own. The purpose of considering shear alongside the residual is to examine whether their relationship helps tell the induced conditions apart.
What would balanced accuracy evaluate here?

It would evaluate the distinction between the grip-slip and odometry-drift conditions. For two conditions, balanced accuracy averages the correct-identification rate for each, rather than letting the more frequent condition dominate an overall accuracy figure. The plan does not provide a measured value, the separate rates, or the number of evaluations.
Should I say the plan achieves at least 90% balanced accuracy?

No. At least 90% balanced accuracy is the proposed performance level for the slip-versus-drift distinction, not an outcome established by this recording-and-evaluation plan. The plan says to evaluate balanced accuracy; it gives no evaluation result.
Does recording FurnitureContact-1 also show that furniture can be repositioned within 5 cm?

Not from what is stated. The plan concerns a recording with induced grip slip and odometry drift during three-second occlusions, followed by fitting shear-conditioned residuals and evaluating balanced accuracy. It does not report repositioning distances or a rate of trials within 5 cm.
Does the plan specify how the induced events will be identified for evaluation?

No. It names the induced conditions and the balanced-accuracy evaluation, but does not describe how condition identities are recorded, how predictions are produced, or how disagreements are handled. Those are not details that should be presented as decisions already made.
Can I infer a particular sensor layout or tracking system from this?

No. Wrist shear is named through the shear-conditioned residuals, and the plan names odometry drift and visual occlusions, but it does not specify sensor placement or an external tracking arrangement. The broader goal requires identification without external tracking during execution; this plan does not provide an implementation account showing how that requirement is met.
Would it be fair to describe this as a test of whether shear helps interpret contact-related inconsistency during occlusion?

Yes, as a description of the intended inquiry rather than a finding. More precisely, the plan is to record FurnitureContact-1 with induced grip slip and odometry drift during three-second visual occlusions, fit residuals conditioned on shear, and evaluate how accurately the two conditions can be distinguished using balanced accuracy.
What should the wording avoid if I want it to remain a plan?

Avoid saying that FurnitureContact-1 has already been recorded, that the residuals have already been fitted, or that balanced accuracy has reached a particular value. The planned sequence is recording the two induced conditions during three-second visual occlusions, fitting shear-conditioned residuals, and evaluating balanced accuracy; its results remain unstated.

The next activity is to run FurnitureContact-1 held-out slip-versus-drift trials with three-second occlusions and compute balanced accuracy from wrist-shear-conditioned contact residuals. What exactly does that ask us to do?

It calls for evaluating the slip-versus-drift distinction on held-out FurnitureContact-1 trials that include three-second visual occlusions. The information used for the distinction is the contact residuals interpreted in relation to wrist shear. Balanced accuracy is the requested evaluation measure. The activity specifies what to run and compute; it does not report that the trials have been run or give an accuracy value.
What does “held-out” add to the evaluation?

It means the trials used to assess the distinction are reserved from the fitting used to form it. That matters because scoring on the same trials used for fitting would not provide the same held-out assessment. The activity does not specify how many trials are reserved or how the reservation is organized.
Should I assume that FurnitureContact-1 has already produced a held-out result?
No. FurnitureContact-1 names the recording involved, and the activity says to run its held-out trials and compute a measure. There is no reported score or completed-trial account in this activity.
What are the two things the held-out trials are meant to distinguish?

Slip and drift. In this context, slip concerns relative movement at the grip, whereas drift concerns an inaccurate pose or motion estimate. The activity evaluates whether the wrist-shear-conditioned contact residuals support that distinction during three-second visual occlusions; it does not state how often either condition appears.
Does “from wrist-shear-conditioned contact residuals” mean classifying from wrist shear alone?

No. Contact residuals are central to that phrase, and wrist shear conditions how they are interpreted. A wrist-shear reading alone is not described as the entire basis for the distinction. The activity also does not provide a formula for the residuals or a rule for combining them with shear.
Could you restate what a contact residual represents in this evaluation?

Conceptually, it represents a mismatch involving the contact relationship and the estimated motion or observations. The activity asks for that mismatch to be considered in light of wrist shear when distinguishing slip from drift. It does not specify the residual’s units, a threshold for calling it present, or a particular mathematical construction.
Are wrist-shear spikes explicitly required in this activity?

The activity specifies wrist-shear-conditioned contact residuals, but it does not explicitly prescribe a spike threshold or say that the evaluation must use a particular spike-detection rule. Its concrete instruction is to run the held-out slip-versus-drift trials and compute balanced accuracy from the conditioned residuals.
Does the three-second condition apply to every held-out trial mentioned here?

The trials called for in the activity are held-out slip-versus-drift trials with three-second occlusions. That duration is part of the specified evaluation condition. The activity does not describe other occlusion durations or say how results would transfer to them.
Does a three-second occlusion mean there is no visual information anywhere in a trial?
No. It identifies a three-second interval of visual occlusion, not an entire trial with no possible visual information. The activity does not state what is visible before or after the interval.
How is balanced accuracy computed for slip versus drift?

For this two-condition distinction, it is the average of the proportion of slip cases correctly identified as slip and the proportion of drift cases correctly identified as drift. That gives each condition equal weight in the measure, regardless of how many held-out cases of each occur. The activity does not provide the counts or either correct-identification rate, so no numerical balanced accuracy can be computed from the statement alone.
Would counting all correct decisions and dividing by all held-out decisions be the same thing?

That would be ordinary overall accuracy. It can differ from balanced accuracy if the two conditions occur in different numbers. The requested computation gives equal weight to the correct-identification rate for slip and the correct-identification rate for drift.
What information would have to be available to compute that measure?

There would need to be a way to determine which held-out cases are slip and which are drift, along with the corresponding classifications from the wrist-shear-conditioned contact residuals. Those are logical requirements of calculating the two correct-identification rates. The activity does not specify how condition identities are established or how a residual-based classification is produced.
Does it say whether a classification is made once per trial or repeatedly within a trial?

No. It names held-out trials as the evaluation setting but does not define the unit at which predictions are made or scored. Claiming a particular decision frequency would add a procedure that is not stated.
Should we assume each held-out trial contains only one of slip and drift?

The activity frames the evaluation as slip versus drift, but it does not describe how trials with ambiguous or simultaneous conditions would be handled. That cannot be inferred merely from the name of the distinction. Any scoring convention for such cases would need to be specified separately.
If the balanced-accuracy calculation is the endpoint, does this activity also measure repositioning accuracy?

Not as stated. The specified computation is balanced accuracy for distinguishing slip from drift using wrist-shear-conditioned contact residuals during the three-second occlusions. The activity supplies no furniture-position error measurements or calculation of how often repositioning finishes within a distance tolerance.
Does “run held-out trials” guarantee that the contact-residual approach generalizes?

No. Held-out evaluation is a way to assess performance on trials not used for fitting; it does not guarantee a particular result or establish performance beyond the conditions evaluated. Here the stated condition is FurnitureContact-1 slip-versus-drift trials with three-second occlusions. The result remains to be computed.
Could an unusually high overall accuracy conceal poor drift identification?

Conceptually, yes, if drift cases were less numerous: overall accuracy could be dominated by correct decisions on the more numerous condition. Balanced accuracy addresses that particular imbalance by averaging the two condition-specific correct-identification rates. It does not, however, reveal both rates on its own; reporting only the average would leave their individual values unknown.
Can I describe this as testing whether a wrist-shear reading directly proves slip?

That would misstate the activity. It evaluates a slip-versus-drift distinction from contact residuals conditioned on wrist shear, not a claim that an isolated wrist-shear reading proves slip. Nor does the activity say that any single residual is conclusive.

Interpreting them together is intended to distinguish physical slip from localization drift, then correct the estimated pose of unseen furniture. This is a proposal, not a reported implementation or result.

Optical flow describes apparent motion in successive observations. Floor-flow odometry uses apparent motion of the floor in a downward-facing view to inform an estimate of the manipulator’s motion relative to that floor. The proposal does not specify the sensing hardware, a calculation, or the accuracy of that estimate.

They concern different parts of the ambiguity. Slip is physical relative movement at the gripper–furniture contact; localization drift is error in an estimated pose. No. Floor flow is information used for odometry: it can reflect motion relative to the floor. Drift concerns error in an estimate. An observation of motion is not, by itself, evidence that the estimate has drifted; the proposal leaves open how the distinction is made.

No. It is still an odometry estimate, not an unquestionable measurement of pose. Its proposed value is as another source of motion information to interpret alongside gripper tactile optical flow. The proposal supplies no accuracy guarantee for either source.

Floor-relative motion information and tactile contact motion could help examine those possibilities, but the proposal provides no decisive signal combination.

Not necessarily. It means they are interpreted together. The proposal does not specify averaging, a factor graph, a filter, numerical weights, or another fusion method. Those would be additional implementation details.

Localization drift: error in the manipulator’s estimate of where it is, as distinct from physical movement at the gripper–furniture contact. The proposal does not identify a cause of drift or specify which component of pose is affected.
